newsitem.title: USA: Bonds end higher, bonds drop before Greenspan testimony.
newsitem.headline: Bonds end higher, bonds drop before Greenspan testimony.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks closed slightly higher, but bonds edged lower on Monday as investors wavered ahead of Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's congressional testimony Tuesday.
The dollar crept higher in very light trade after a French public sector audit fuelled speculation that Europe's planned single currency will be weak.

The Dow Jones industrial average rose 16.26 points to 7,906.72, stabilising after Friday's 130-point drop. But declining issues swamped advances, 1,910 to 950, on the New York Stock Exchange, where volume was moderate at 459 million shares.
"I think people are kind of resting before the next wave," said James Volk, director of trading at Jensen Securities.
More profit taking, especially in technology stocks, clipped the tech-heavy Nasdaq composite index, which fell 11.76 points to 1,536.23.

But many investors appeared to be awaiting results from International Business Machines Corp., which reported after the market closed that it earned $1.4 billion, or $1.46 a share, in the second quarter, up from $1.3 billion, or $1.26 a share, a year earlier.
Traders said the computer maker's results, which were in line with analysts' estimates of $1.42 a share, according to First Call, could help sooth some recent investor nervousness.
"I don't think there's any shock here either way," said Guy Truicko, equity portfolio manger at Unity Management. "But the fact is that they beat the number."

On Tuesday, Wall Street will be weighing comments from Greenspan on the direction of the economy, interest rates or the stock market itself. The central bank chairman will deliver his semi-annual testimony to Congress on Tuesday and Wednesday.
Analysts said they expect the Fed chief to say the central bank needs to be wary of inflation, despite recent economic data showing muted price rises.
"The market will likely be on hold on the downside until we get through Greenspan," said Richard Cripps, chief market strategist at Legg Mason Wood Walker.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond fell 5/32, or $1.5625 on a $1,000 bond, raising its yield to 6.54 percent from 6.52 percent on Friday's close.
The dollar ended at 1.7960 German marks, up from 1.7925 late Friday. The dollar also rose to 116.15 Japanese yen from Friday's closing rate of 115.60.
Corn prices fell as rain soaked key growing areas in the U.S. Midwest, boosting prospects for this year's crop.
CBOT corn for September delivery closed 7-1/4 cents a bushel lower at $2.45-1/4 a bushel after at one staging falling its 12-cent limit to $2.40-1/2.

At the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, lumber futures closed the $10 per thousand board feet lower, weakened partly by the absence of any major damage to properties in the Southeast from Hurricane Danny.
CME lumber for September delivery closed the $10 per thousand board feet lower at $351.

At the New York Mercantile Exchange, crude oil futures closed lower, sagging under losses in gasoline prices and a possible of surge in Iraqi oil exports once the oil for food deal restarts. August crude ended 9 cents a barrel off at $19.18. August gasoline settled off 0.01 cent a gallon at 60.04 cents while August heating oil finished 0.13 cent up at 52.35 cents a gallon.
Overseas, London's FTSE 100 closed at 4,805.7, down 71.5 points, or 1.47 percent. Japan's financial markets were closed for a national holiday.
